Yesterday, designer-couturier-jewellery maker, Sabyasachi Mukherjee opened his new store in Delhi. Spread across 26,000 square feet, is his largest yet in India. It has approximately 120 chandeliers, hundreds of artworks, antique carpets, textiles, mirrors and decorative objects. Over the years as Sabyasachi designed and redesigned his stores, adding spaces and retail categories, his visual language, obsession with oldness and his ability to turn nostalgia into desire became the stuff of writing.

It is hard to write a piece if you can’t breathe between the description of the objects that are the designer’s subjects. The tiger on the prowl in these rooms is not only the wild cat of Bengal that Sabyasachi is so intensely fond of but the problem of making sense of “more”. 

But what struck me for the first time was a sense of control in the curation of these museum-like stores. Look closely and nothing is chaotic. They are crowded with objects, but they are not confused. Each corridor leads the eye to somewhere else. Every room reveals another. There is clear choreography.

I had only one question for Sabyasachi. “How do you respond to a space that has nothing on it, is blank, without any colour, decoration or ornamentation? How does emptiness make you feel?”

Before blinking or breathing, he said “You are talking about my bedroom in my home in Kolkata.” It’s is bare. There is nothing on the walls. Nothing anywhere in it. “All this is my armour, my mask, my makeup, my theatre. This is not me. I am a minimalist at heart; a maximalist as a creator.”

Which is why, after walking through 26,000 square feet of Sabyasachi, I keep thinking about his room in Kolkata that he described to me with nothing on the walls.

What does rap have to do with handloom? Quite a bit, says Sanjay Garg, founder-designer of Raw Mango. The brand dropped a track this morning on Instagram in which tennis-player-turned-rapper Adil Kalyanpur belts out words like jamdani, ikat and brocade—and what nobody ever told “you” about why handlooms matter. The “you”, one hopes, is the young.
Kalyanpur, aka A-KAL, is Gen Z. More enjoyably, Garg says, he knew almost nothing about handlooms before the Raw Mango team approached him. In the rap, weaving vocabulary gets rhyme, rhythm and swagger.
The song, written by Garg and his team, is “osm”, as the young like to say. What it implies may not be as breezy. The foot tapping number leads to three subjects that Garg believes matter at the moment: jobs, identity and climate.
On the phone yesterday, the ever-passionate, breathlessly persuasive Garg described the rap as another addition to what Raw Mango has been stacking up around National Handloom Day over the years. Books, songs, stars and actors wearing Raw Mango—each year, he looks for another way in. Handloom Day, he insists, cannot only be about wearables or fashion. Nor is Garg interested in purist pursuits. He would rather “argue, disrupt, disagree” than service a familiar formula.
That is where the rap becomes more than a clever Handloom Day social media post. 
For years, India’s handloom conversations—including many we find today—have circled around three exhortations: wear it, buy it, praise the artisan. Handloom is positioned as ethical duty. All remain important, of course. But handloom cannot survive on worthiness alone. It must expand into other territories to become a loom of ideas, not just cloth.
Handloom is circular. Yet, given the chance, it can also soar or sing.
Garg does want us to know, though, that the rap was conceptualised and shot before the student protests taught us so vividly how to remain circular and fly.

British designer John Galliano’s return to mainstream fashion has unfolded in carefully calibrated acts: a 2013 residency at Oscar de la Renta, his appointment at Maison Margiela in 2014 and the Spring 2024 Artisanal show that became a viral sensation and reaffirmed his formidable talents as a couturier. Kevin Macdonald’s documentary High & Low—John Galliano followed, and in March came a two-year partnership with Zara to “re-author” its archives.
Now, comes the ultimate benediction: John Galliano: Horizons, the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition. Galliano will become the third living designer, after Yves Saint Laurent and Rei
Kawakubo, to be conferred this honour. A solo Met exhibition places a designer in fashion history; the gala turns it into global spectacle. And while Galliano is a compelling subject, he’s a treacherous one. In 2011, he
was dismissed from Dior and his eponymous label after uttering antisemitic and racist remarks and was later convicted by a French court. The Met says it will
confront this problematic history in an opening section ‘Bearings’. Curator Andrew Bolton has rejected a simple fall-and-redemption narrative, focusing instead on the tension between creative achievement and accountability. While Galliano’s romantic vagabonds, bias-cut heroines and theatrical Dior fantasies offer great dress-code material, will the evening devolve into an
absolving tribute? Or will ’Bearings’ serve as a neutral disclaimer to an exhibit devoted to a “disgraced” genius?
Met Gala’s lead chairperson Anna Wintour has been a long-time supporter of Galliano, but Bolton claims a more scholarly engagement, spanning years of writing and exhibitions. Reports say the duo and Galliano have met Jewish leaders and the Anti-Defamation League has acknowledged his apology and atonement. That context matters. Galliano’s contribution to fashion is too significant to erase, but his former misdemeanour can’t be reduced to a footnote in a triumphant career narrative. Can the Met Gala’s machinery of spectacle hold accountability without turning it into another theme, or is redemption already written on the horizon?

We, the people of India, are now highly literate in the language of public relations. We know what a statement sounds like when every potentially “troublesome” noun has been removed from it. We recognise that words like “healing”, “unity”, “our youth”, “coming together” and “difficult times” tell us what the person issuing them actually thinks. Nothing much.

Back in the day, we loved stars enough to write letters in blood, fast and pray for them, queue outside their homes for a glimpse or a touch. We bought movie tickets, copied haircuts and clothes, and bought products because famous faces told us to.

In return, celebrities gave us glamour, fantasy and that mysterious substance called stardom.
Social media dismantled much of that arrangement. Celebrity became content.
Now, the student protests of 2026 have exposed the consequence of that shift. Audiences no longer want only access to celebrities. They want to know what they stand for.

After all, every Instagram follower is an economic asset. Every fan is a potential cinema ticket, streaming view, endorsement consumer or amplifier. Celebrities ask audiences to care about their films, fashion, fitness, beauty brands, holidays, causes and lives.

It becomes increasingly difficult to tell those same audiences that public or political life is none of their business when something genuinely consequential occurs.
Young fans are asking a brutally simple question: If you want our attention when you are selling something, where are you when we need yours?

The Indian star has not fallen. Glamour is not going anywhere, and neither is fandom. But celebrity exceptionalism may finally be weakening.
The chasm between actors Naseeruddin Shah and Kangana Ranaut—the latter also a politician—in their apparent socio-political convictions and articulation is so wide that it is unlikely to ever close. India will clap for Virat Kohli when he scores runs for the country. But in our heart of hearts, we also know Kohli is unlikely to wear his heart on his sleeve when it comes to the right to protest.
